This paper proposes a novel framework for unsupervised time series representation learning that avoids augmentation by leveraging frame projections. The method provides an elegant mathematical formulation, grounded in signal processing, and demonstrates strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks.

Reviewers appreciated the clarity of presentation, the solid theoretical underpinnings, and the meaningful improvements over competitive baselines. Strengths noted include the elegant solution to a problem typically addressed with heuristics, and the consistent empirical gains. Concerns raised centered on the choice of baselines, missing comparisons with some recent methods, and clarity regarding certain transformations.

The authors provided a detailed and constructive rebuttal, adding new experimental comparisons, clarifying methodological details, and addressing reviewer questions on baselines, mappings, and related work. Reviewers acknowledged these efforts positively in the discussion, and their updated assessments reflected increased confidence.

Overall, this submission presents a clear, technically sound, and impactful contribution to self-supervised learning for time series. The reviewers’ feedback, the thorough author response, and the subsequent discussion collectively support acceptance.

rebuttal.value:
We would like to thank the reviewer for their time and recognizing the importance of the problem. We have addressed each point below.

**Theoretical justification**

We agree with the reviewer. Our Proposition, which shows the geometries of the latent spaces can be different, is the theoretical motivation for the proposed mappers but not the overall method.
We understand the importance of theoretical justification for SSL but the overall method is complex so we could not perform a rigorous mathematical verification. We can conjecture that our method works without collapsing because of the implicit bias exposed by the applied frame projections and their encoders. As per the reviewer’s suggestion, we have added a concise explanation at the end of our response to explain why NT‑Xent loss combined with transforms does not induce (undesired) invariances.


**Vision-Language**

We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. Our method is motivated by the diverse data augmentation strategies in time series applications while depending on the task. In the vision domain, cropping and color augmentations are well established and widely used. Also, the design of encoders for frame projections requires additional careful modifications on the architectures. We acknowledge this and will mention it as an avenue for future work in the revised version.


**Hyperparameters**

We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We have tried several hyperparameters for Barlow Twins, however, we have observed no significant change in the performance of the models, and mostly got worse when the value increased. This is consistent with the original paper, where the authors conducted an ablation study and found the method to be stable across a range of hyperparameter settings.

Regarding the other baselines, we use their original hyperparameters as specified for each application. For example, TS-TCC adjusts augmentation parameters depending on the task (e.g., activity recognition vs. sleep staging), and we follow those settings exactly. We believe this highlights the value of our approach as it performs consistently well across all datasets and applications without requiring task-specific hyperparameter tuning.


**Standard deviation, significance**

While some methods come close on individual datasets, our approach consistently achieves the top rank across all tasks. For instance, TF‑C performs strongly on ECG datasets (ranking second to our method) but its accuracy falls to about 30% on the activity recognition task. In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we generated a critical difference (CD) diagram using the Friedman Chi‑Square test (significance at p < 0.05). For each task, we randomly sample from the confidence intervals 1,000 times, apply CD ranking, and average the results. The CD analysis confirms that our method is statistically superior to the alternatives. We thank the reviewer for the feedback to make the significance clearer, and we will include these new results in the revised manuscript.


**Figures 3-4**

In Figures 3 and 4, the standard deviations were very small relative to the means, resulting in error bars that were not visually noticeable. For example, in Figure 3–4(a), the deviation was less than 0.1% of the mean, and around 1% in Figure 3–4(b). For clarity, we initially excluded them in figures. We will explain this exclusion in the revised script.

**Related works**

We discuss augmentation-free SSL in Appendix G (Expanded Related Work, **page 33**). We will include the suggested reference in the revised version while noting that it relies on equivariant network architectures.

**Questions**

1. We thank the reviewer for the careful reading. We will add the definition in the revision.

2. We thank the reviewer for this important question. While we could not identify any specific known invariances, we conjecture that combining the NT‑Xent loss with a unitary basis transformation inherently forces the encoder to preserve features. In our framework, positive pairs differ only by a basis change, so every inner product, and therefore every pairwise relationship, remains exactly the same.

    In contrast, conventional SSL augmentations (for example, color vs. texture distortions) unevenly warp different subspaces. This uneven distortion lets the model minimize its loss by selectively ignoring or emphasizing certain features, which can introduce blind spots or unwanted invariances [2]. Because our transforms apply a uniform change across the entire feature space, there is no incentive for the encoder to drop or over‑emphasize any subset of features.


3. We have explained the Manifold term on Appendix A.1.2 on **page 16** with the manifold hypothesis assumption. We will revise the script to refer the section with manifold hypothesis and related references for normalized embedding spaces [1].

4. We thank the reviewer for the suggestion. We have included the suggested reference and are happy to cover any other work we have missed in Appendix G. Since we could not find any known invariances the model induce, we are also happy to try and see specific ones if the reviewer has any suggestions.

5. Since the frame projections require special design of architectures that operate with complex numbers, we have left the vision domain as a future work.

6. We agree with the reviewer and will revise it by indicating an average difference of ~15% with the second best method (TS2Vec according to the CD).


**Preventing invariances**

**Perfect alignment**

From [3], at the NT‑Xent optimum, perfect alignment across positive pairs is expected;

$$
f^\*_{ \mathcal{F} }(\mathcal{F} (x) ) = f^\*(x)
$$

**Extra invariance**

Suppose now that the encoder also becomes invariant to some unintended transformation $W$:

$$
f^\*(W x ) = f^\*(x)
$$

Then for anchor $x$ consider the contrastive loss (omitting the temperature term for simplicity):

$$
\ell(x)= -\log\frac{\exp(f^\*(x) \cdot f^\ast_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}(x)))}
{\exp(f^\*(x) \cdot f^\ast_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{F}(x))) + \sum_{\begin{array}{c} \text{all} \\ \text{negatives} \end{array}}
\exp\bigl(f^\*(x) \cdot z_{\rm neg}\bigr)}
$$

Because of the invariance, there are at least $K\ge1$ negatives
$\{z_i = f^\*(W x_i)}_{i=1}^K$
with
$\langle f^*(x) \,z_i\rangle \approx 1$.
Even if all other negatives were perfectly dissimilar, the denominator contains at least $K+1$ terms $e^{1/\tau}$, so

$$
\ell(x)\ge-\log\frac{e^{1/\tau}}{(K+1)\,e^{1/\tau}}=\log(K+1)>0.
$$

Hence, whenever multiple negatives become near‐positives through any unintended invariance, NT‑Xent in our setup cannot be driven to zero. In contrast, prior contrastive learning setups encourage the encoder to learn augmentation-induced invariances (i.e., drop or over-emphasize certain features in order to reduce the loss for positive pairs).

While the assumption of optimal encoders is strong, it is consistent with prior theoretical works in contrastive learning, which also adopt this viewpoint to analyze properties [1,3].

[1] Understanding Contrastive Representation Learning through Alignment and Uniformity on the Hypersphere. ICML 2020.

[2] Views Can Be Deceiving: Improved SSL Through Feature Space Augmentation. ICLR 2024.

[3] Chaos is a Ladder: A New Theoretical Understanding of Contrastive Learning via Augmentation Overlap. ICLR 2022.

Once again, we sincerely thank the reviewer for their insightful comments and suggestions, as well as for highlighting the invariant features and statistical significance, which have contributed to strengthening the quality of our work.

We would like to thank the reviewer for taking their time and feedback. We have addressed each question below. 

**Relevant works**

We would like to thank the reviewer for pointing out Timesurl. In the limited time, we have evaluated its performance in challenging heart rate estimation datasets which include severe noise. Our method outperforms the timesurl by ~8–9%, as shown in the table below (using the correlation metric $\rho$).

| Method        | SPC12            | SPC22            | DaLiA            |
|---------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Timesurl | 75.13$\pm$1.22   | 50.10$\pm$1.97 | 60.17$\pm$0.11 |
| **Ours**  | **82.67$\pm$1.30** | **54.88$\pm$1.89** | **63.72$\pm$0.06** |

We observed that Timesurl applies significant modifications in the frequency domain for augmentations which can change the characteristics of the signal. We will extend the experiments to other datasets and include the results in revision.

**Ablations on mapping function**

We have included several ablations about mapping functions in Appendix D on **page 23**.

**Forecasting**

We would like to thank the reviewer for this question. We mainly focused on classification as the data augmentations are more diverse and challenging, where even specific augmentations are developed [4-5]. But, since our method uses global (FFT) and local (Gabor) representations together for learning, it can be useful for forecasting tasks as well. We will add this discussion to the manuscript. 

**Fine tuning**

We have provided the fine tuning results in Appendix D.4. on **page 24-25**.

**Questions**

1) We have included initial experiments related to the referenced Timesurl and we will expand them in the revision. Regarding [2], the authors used mixup instead of traditional augmentations, but prior work [4] has shown that simple mixup strategies often underperform on time series data. We also thank the reviewer for highlighting [3], which introduces random projection heads to generate pseudo targets and uses predictors trained with a Barlow Twins–style loss. While conceptually interesting, we found that Barlow Twins tends to perform poorly in noisy settings such as heart rate estimation, as its emphasis on decorrelating feature components can cause the model to amplify noise.

rebuttal.value:
We would like to thank the reviewer for their detailed feedback and for listing their questions, which we have addressed below. We also appreciate their recognition of the novelty and the significance of our proposed solution.

**Supervised references**
We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. Our goal was to ensure a fair comparison by using baselines with similar model capacity and training data. Since our method does not rely on data augmentation, we also demonstrate that it performs well with effectively less data. In line with standard practice in self-supervised learning, we use the same backbone across methods to isolate the effect of architectures. While recent foundation models like LaBraM, EEGPT, and CBraMod show strong results, they typically rely on much larger architectures and huge pretraining datasets, making a direct comparison less meaningful in our setup. 

Nonetheless, per the reviewer's suggestion, we have used the pre-trained weights (from Huggingface) of CBraMod (the most recent work) to evaluate on Sleep-EDF. We extract features using model’s pretrained weights, then either train only a linear classifier or fine‑tune the full network on the same training split of Sleep‑EDF. We reported the results below.

| **Method**           | **Linear evaluation** | **Fine‑tuning** |
| -------------------- | --------------------- | --------------- |
| CBraMod (pretrained) | 65.03$\\pm$0.63   | **72.98$\\pm$0.47**  |
| Ours        | **69.19$\\pm$1.32**  | 71.13$\\pm$0.84        |

We followed this evaluation scheme to isolate and compare the learned representations. It is also important to note that CBraMod was not originally trained on single‑channel EEG, which may contribute to observed performance discrepancies in linear evaluation. Additionally, CBraMod uses a transformer layer for sequence‑to‑sequence sleep staging, whereas we applied a linear classifier to ensure a fair comparison with other representation learning methods, such as TS-TCC. We will include these implementation details and the extended evaluation protocol in the revised manuscript.

**Processing times**
 A key advantage of our approach is that the FFT and Gabor transform computations can be performed once and cached, enabling efficient training. In contrast, traditional augmentations are applied at every epoch, introducing repeated computational overhead. To clarify this, we report runtimes (measured on an NVIDIA RTX 4090) for a batch of 1024 samples using FFT (implemented with `PyTorch`), Gabor transforms (via the `pywt` library), and two common temporal augmentations (permutation and scale + noise, implemented with `NumPy`). Although we also experimented with implementing augmentations in `PyTorch` for speed, we did not observe significant differences in runtime.

| **Transform** | **Runtime (s)---1 epoch**   | **Runtime (s)---500 epochs**  |
| ------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------- |
| FFT           | 0.0075                 |    0.0075       |
| Gabor         | 3.59                   |  3.59       |
| Permutation   | 0.021 × *epoch\_count* |      10.5     |
| Scale + Noise | 0.010 × *epoch\_count* |       5  |

Considering that SSL methods typically train for ~300-500 [1], up to 1000 epochs, our approach becomes significantly more computationally efficient than augmentations, with approximately a 4× speedup at 500 epochs, due to its one-time preprocessing cost.


**Questions**

1) We evaluated the EEG-based sleep classification task using the pretrained weights from one of the suggested foundational models. However, It is again important to note that the fairness of a direct comparison is controversial as both model size (i.e., CBraMod has 20x more parameters than our backbone) and training data of the foundational models are huge compared to our approach. In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we have added a discussion and detailed comparison between this foundational model and our approach.
2) We confirmed that the performance decreases significantly when we use linear mappers. We conducted this experiment and reported in Appendix D.2 on **page 23**.
3) When we trained the mappers and encoders all together, we observed a decrease in the performance, and we hypothesized that the gradients from mappers could force encoders to a simple solution for making the mapping easier. We thank the reviewer for this question, we will include that ablation in Appendix as well.
4) We thank the reviewer for raising this important question. The transformations we use, FFT and Gabor, are not straightforward for models to learn or invert, as they involve complex exponentials with high-frequency components. Specifically, in the case of the FFT, inverting the transformation requires a full linear mapping over all input dimensions; this is not achievable unless the encoder can represent a dense $D \times D$ matrix, where $D$ is the input dimension. Multi-layer convolutional encoder with small receptive fields *cannot* implement such a transform unless its total receptive field spans the full input. Gabor transforms are even more complex, involving both time shifts and frequency modulations, which further increase the difficulty of exact inversion.


    We conjecture that these transforms expose complementary structures in the data (e.g., global trends via FFT, localized patterns via Gabor), which encourages the model to learn representations rather than collapsing into trivial solutions.

    We agree that a low-dimensional toy example could be helpful for intuition. However, due to the inherently high-dimensional nature of these transforms, such examples may oversimplify and fail to reflect the true dynamics. Thus, we will include a verbal explanation and expand on this intuition in the revision, as suggested.


[1] A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations. ICML 2020.


We thank the reviewer again for their time and for helping us improve the clarity and depth of our work.

summary.value: This paper notes that most SSL approaches require handcrafted augmentations, which need to be optimized for specific downstream tasks and are not necessarily generalizable. To address this they propose a novel approach where they do instance discrimination after a projection step. They use several representations of their data and train an encoder for each domain. I was actually a bit confused after that by Figure 1 and its description, but my understanding is that after multiple mappings they have a separate embedding for each branch. They then compute instancewise discrimination loss between the branches over a batch for neighboring points. Finally, they show that their method outperforms several well known classic SSL techniques on a number of benchmarks.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
# Strengths
- very clear. I am less familiar with frames and manifolds, so I appreciated how you provided a lot of intuition. I appreciated how e.g. proposition 2.1 had intuition before the statement of the proposition.
- mathematically elegant solution to an important problem, previously mostly solved by heuristics. Further, it’s tied well to the applications.
- One sees a large improvement over baselines.

# Weaknesses
- The baselines are more classic than SOTA and largely come from a few years ago. This makes the method potentially look better than it is. I’m forgiving a bit of this because the technique is elegant, but really, you should use harder baselines.
- the datasets are also a bit older, but since there are a good number of them that is ok.

Overall, I see this as worth publishing as it is an elegant, interesting method that performs at least reasonably against more classic baselines. Future work could be trying to push these sorts of ideas towards SOTA on competitive modern benchmarks.

summary.value: This paper introduces a self-supervised learning framework that learns from three invertible transformations of each time-series example: raw signal, full FFT coefficients, and Gabor-wavelet frame, each encoded separately. Each pair of domains are applied with InfoNCE loss. Two tiny MLP mappers predict the frequency-domain embeddings from the time-domain embedding. In inference only the time encoder and the mappers are needed. On 9 ECG / EEG/ PPG / IMU datasets, the method surpasses SimCLR-style and other time-series-specific baselines by 30 %.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
The strengths are 1. The information-preserving design removes the need for hand-crafted augmentations. 2. The “coordinate consistency as (self) supervision” is novel and could potentially generalize to vision or audio.



Weaknesses are 
1. Supervised references for EEG / ECG are outdated. Recent foundation models such as LaBraM, EEGPT, and CBraMod report strong numbers; comparison or discussion is required.

Jiang et al., 2024, “LaBraM: Large Brain Model for Learning Generic Representations with Tremendous EEG Data”.
Yue et al., 2024, “EEGPT: Unleashing the Potential of EEG Generalist Foundation Model by Autoregressive Pre-training”.
Wang et al., 2024, “CBraMod: A Criss-Cross Brain Foundation Model for EEG Decoding”.

2. The paper misses the preprocessing time of the FFT + Gabor transforms. A simple wall-clock benchmark on the largest dataset—ideally side-by-side with the run-time of the common augmentation pipeline used by SimCLR-style baselines—would make the compute overhead clear.

questions.value:
- Can you add frozen-encoder baselines from LaBraM, EEGPT, and CBraMod, or explain why their checkpoints cannot run on your datasets?
- Mapper ablation: what happens when each 500-parameter MLP is replaced by a linear layer?
- Have you tried joint training in which mappers and encoders are optimised together? If so, what are the results?
- Can the authors explain intuitively why this works? For instance, in a toy example where one view is cartesian coordinates and the other is polar, a polar-view encoder could trivially apply the known mapping from cartesian to polar. By analogy, why doesn’t your protocol collapse into each encoder simply inverting the other view? A concise, low-dimension explanation would help readers grasp where the learning signal comes from. summary.value: The paper addresses the task of time series self-supervised learning (SSL). The authors propose a novel augmentation-free SSL method. Specifically, the method eliminates the need for traditional data augmentation by leveraging Fourier and Gabor wavelet transforms as additional views alongside the original input. In addition, the authors introduce a mapping function from the time domain to these transformed views during training to facilitate more efficient inference. The proposed method is evaluated on several time series classification tasks and datasets, where it outperforms existing augmentation-based SSL methods.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
- The authors effectively highlight the challenge of designing hand-crafted augmentations, which makes the proposed augmentation-free approach highly relevant.
- The paper is well-written, with particularly clear definitions of notations and methodology. The approach is easy to follow and understand.
- To the best of my knowledge, this is the first work that utilizes Fourier and Gabor wavelet transforms for time series self-supervised learning (SSL), contributing new methods to the field.
- Comprehensive Experimentation: The authors conduct an extensive set of experiments across a variety of tasks and datasets. The comparison between larger backbones and multiple views for the baseline methods (L198-L201) is insightful and provides a fair evaluation of the proposed method.

Weakness
- Some relevant works are missing: 
  - The paper does not discuss more recent work on time series contrastive self-supervised learning (SSL), such as Timesurl [1], which shows to outperform some of the included baselines. 
  - Other relevant research on augmentation-free SSL methods, such as [2] and [3], is not discussed or compared. 
- The mapping function is an important part of the work, but the effect of its accuracy is not discussed. 
- The paper lacks a discussion on the applicablity of the proposed method on ftime-series forecasting tasks.
- The paper focuses evaluation on linear probing only without finetuning experiments, which is another popular way for testing representation quality.

[1] Liu, J. and Chen, S., 2024, March. "Timesurl: Self-supervised contrastive learning for universal time series representation learning." In Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (Vol. 38, No. 12, pp. 13918-13926).
[2]Verma, V., Luong, T., Kawaguchi, K., Pham, H. and Le, Q., 2021, July. Towards domain-agnostic contrastive learning. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 10530-10541). PMLR.
[3] Sui, Y., Wu, T., Cresswell, J.C., Wu, G., Stein, G., Huang, X.S., Zhang, X. and Volkovs, M., 2023. Self-supervised representation learning from random data projectors. arXiv preprint arXiv:2310.07756.

- Could you discuss relevant works that are not covered in the paper?
- What is the effect of the learned mapping function’s accuracy on the overall performance?
- Does the proposed SSL method work on forecasting tasks?
- Would it be possible to include fine-tuning experimental results as well?

final_justification.value:
In my original review, I raised several concerns regarding the completeness and positioning of the paper:
- The experimental baselines were not sufficiently recent or competitive.
- The related work lacked discussion of domain-agnostic or augmentation-free self-supervised learning (SSL) methods across modalities.
- The method was only evaluated on time-series classification, with no discussion on its applicability to forecasting tasks.

In the rebuttal, the authors provided a thoughtful response and acknowledged these limitations. Specifically:
- They committed to incorporating more advanced and recent baselines in future revisions.
- They agreed to include and discuss augmentation-free SSL methods across modalities, both as baselines and in the related work.
- They clarified that the proposed framework is not limited to classification and can generalize to forecasting tasks, and they will include this discussion in future versions.

Given these clarifications and commitments, I believe the paper shows stronger potential than initially assessed. While some improvements remain to be implemented, the response indicates a clear path forward. Based on this, I have raised my score.

summary.value: The authors propose to use projections of the data into Fourier space and Gabor wavelet space as 'views' for self supervised learning, in-place of traditional augmentations. They show empirically that this method improves performance slightly across a range of time-series datasets and compared with a diverse set of SSL benchmarks.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
**Strengths:**
- The proposed problem is important and well motivated. Indeed, data-specific augmentations are one of the big limitations of modern SSL methods, especially when applying them to data domains outside of images or text. Therefore, methods to alleviate this need for hand-crafted augmentations are highly valuable. Additionally, the overall insight that different frames can be used in place of these augmentations is an interesting and valuable one.
- The experimental results are strong, showing broadly improved performance on many tasks, and increased performance at a range of model sizes. 
- The authors perform a set of ablations to validate their modeling choices, which is a welcome addition.


**Weaknesses**
- The theoretical understanding provided to justify the method is quite limited.
- The experimental evaluation is focused on time-series modeling, while the most prominent SSL methods are used for vision and language -- yet the authors make no mention of these domains in the text. The authors should at least acknowledge this fact, and describe why or if their method does not work on such domains, or if they do not know, rather than ignoring this application. 
- It appears the authors re-trained all baseline methods from scratch in their reported results since the datasets they used are not the traditional SSL benchmarks the methods were developed on. It is not clear that in this process the baselines were tuned properly. There are many possible parameter settings, and with so many baselines, tuning would appear challenging. For Barlow Twins for example, the authors report using the hyperparameter lambda to 0.005 without any tuning. These details can have a significant effect on performance. If the authors could find any published results from prior work on these datasets that would be beneficial to increase confidence in their results.
- The performance standard deviation on many experiments seem quite large relative to the differences in model mean performance, yet the authors have no statistical significance indications. 
- The figures 3 and 4 are missing error bars despite the tables having them.
- The related work section is missing some related work which also studies self-superivsed learning without augmentations. One particularly related method is "Homomorphic Self-Supervised Learning" (Keller, Suau, Zappella, 2023 TMLR).

questions.value:
- The `t` domain is not defined prior to equation (2). 
- The authors note that SSL often results in models which are overly reliant on a subsset of features, or an undesirably invariant to a subset of features. How does using othonormal basis fix this other than the fact that the specific invariances may be harder to intuit now? 
- Can the authors justify the use of the term 'manifold'? It is not immediately clear that these representation spaces are manifolds in the formal sense. 
- A more extensive coverage of prior work specifically related to 'augmentation-free SSL', and an improved theoretical understanding of the proposed approach would be beneficial. For example, if the authors can formalize or empirically measure the types of invariances that their proposed projects would induce, this would greatly increase the impact of the work. 
- The proposed approach seems amenable to image SSL representation learning as well. Have the authors experimented with this?
- The claim of 'up to 20-30%' performance increase seems a bit misleading given the difference in performance on many datasets is relatively small. I would encourage the authors to make the claim more quantitative and informative of the actual distribution of results.

limitations.value: The authors should mention if or why there method was not evaluated in image settings.

final_justification.value: The paper is an interesting method, applied to an interesting problem (augmentation-free SSL) that appears to work well. The main limitations of the paper are a lack of theoretical backing, and limited empirical evaluation (such as on vision tasks) that the authors have described as future work. We therefore think the reasons to accept the paper outweighs the reasons to reject marginally, since the paper is interesting, technically correct, and well written, but could have significant improvements with further development. .

title.value: Learning Without Augmenting: Unsupervised Time Series Representation Learning via Frame Projections

abstract.value: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for learning representations without labeled data. Most SSL approaches rely on strong, well-established, handcrafted data augmentations to generate diverse views for representation learning. However, designing such augmentations requires domain-specific knowledge and implicitly imposes representational invariances on the model, which can limit generalization. In this work, we propose an unsupervised representation learning method that replaces augmentations by generating views using orthonormal bases and overcomplete frames. We show that embeddings learned from orthonormal and overcomplete spaces reside on distinct manifolds, shaped by the geometric biases introduced by representing samples in different spaces. By jointly leveraging the complementary geometry of these distinct manifolds, our approach achieves superior performance without artificially increasing data diversity through strong augmentations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on nine datasets across five temporal sequence tasks, where signal-specific characteristics make data augmentations particularly challenging. Without relying on augmentation-induced diversity, our method achieves performance gains of up to 15--20\% over existing self-supervised approaches. Source code: \url{https://github.com/eth-siplab/Learning-with-FrameProjections}
